chapters.title: Chapter 5: Owning Real Estate Without Buying Property

lessons.title: REITs: Listed Office Parks and Malls on NSE and BSE

children.text: The office parks where Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Microsoft run their Indian operations are some of the best commercial real estate in the country. For decades, only developers, global funds and the very rich could own a piece of them. Today, you can buy a slice of those same buildings on NSE or BSE for a few hundred rupees, receive a share of the rent every quarter, and sell it the next day. That is what a REIT does. This lesson explains how they work, what they pay, and what can go wrong.

body.text: A REIT turns large, rent-earning buildings into small, tradable units. You give up control over a specific property, and in return you get diversification, professional management, regular income and the ability to sell in a day.

markDefs.definition: Real Estate Investment Trust: a SEBI-regulated trust that owns mostly completed, rent-earning properties and distributes most of its cash flows to unitholders.
Special Purpose Vehicle: a company set up to hold a specific property or group of properties, owned by the REIT.
The entity, usually a developer or global investment firm, that sets up the REIT, contributes the initial properties and must hold a minimum stake.

The Rules That Make REITs Different

markDefs.definition: Net Distributable Cash Flows: the cash left from rent after operating costs, interest and tax, which forms the base for REIT distributions.

children.text: SEBI's REIT Regulations, first issued in 2014, are designed to keep REITs focused on steady rental income rather than speculative development:

body.caption: Key SEBI rules for listed REITs (simplified)

cells: At least 80% of assets in completed, rent-earning properties
Your money is mostly in buildings with tenants, not construction risk
At least 90% of net distributable cash flows distributed
Most of the rent reaches you instead of being retained
Borrowing capped, with a hard ceiling of 49% of asset value
Limits how much leverage the REIT can take on
An estimated value per unit is published for comparison with the market price
Units trade on NSE and BSE, with a trading lot of one unit
You can invest small amounts and sell on any trading day
Treated as equity for mutual fund investment from 1 January 2026
More mutual fund money can flow in, and REITs became eligible for equity indices from 1 July 2026

body.title: The payout rule
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires listed REITs to distribute at least ___% of their net distributable cash flows to unitholders.
body.explanation: The 90% rule is why REITs behave like income investments. Most of the rent collected is passed through to unitholders rather than retained for expansion.

children.text: Like a flat, a REIT has two engines of return: distributions, which work like rent, and changes in the unit price, which work like appreciation. The distribution yield is the easiest number to compare with a rented flat or an FD.

body.latex: \text{Distribution Yield} = \frac{\text{Distributions per Unit over 12 Months}}{\text{Current Unit Price}} \times 100
body.caption: Because the unit price changes daily, the yield changes too. A falling price raises the yield on new purchases, and vice versa.

body.title: Calculate a distribution yield
body.prompt: A REIT unit trades at ₹380. It paid ₹5.40, ₹5.60, ₹5.70 and ₹5.70 per unit over the last four quarters. What is its distribution yield, in %? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Total distributions: ₹5.40 + ₹5.60 + ₹5.70 + ₹5.70 = ₹22.40. Yield: ₹22.40 ÷ ₹380 = 5.89%. Compare that with the 1.8% to 2.5% net yield many rented flats earn after costs and tax.

markDefs.definition: The estimated value of a REIT's properties minus its debt, divided by the number of units. A unit price below NAV means the market values the REIT below its independent valuation.
Weighted Average Lease Expiry: the average time left on a REIT's leases, weighted by rent. A longer WALE means more predictable income.

What REITs solve, and what they do not

columns.label: Problems REITs solve
points: High ticket size and concentration in one property
Stamp duty and heavy transaction costs

columns.label: Risks that remain
points: Unit prices fall when interest rates rise, like bond prices
Offices depend on corporate hiring and occupancy; malls depend on consumer spending
Distributions are not guaranteed and can be cut
Sponsors may have conflicts of interest in related-party deals
Only a handful of REITs exist, mostly offices, so sector diversification is limited

body.text: REIT distributions are not all taxed the same way. Each payout is split into components such as interest, dividend and repayment of debt, and each component can be taxed differently. REITs publish this breakdown every quarter. For investors in higher tax slabs, the after-tax yield can be noticeably lower than the headline yield, so check the breakdown and confirm the treatment with a tax professional.

body.title: Why did the price fall?
body.question: An office REIT raised its quarterly distribution, and occupancy stayed stable. Yet its unit price fell 8% over three months. What is the most likely reason?
options: The REIT must have hidden losses
Interest rates rose, making fixed-income alternatives more attractive than REIT yields
REIT prices always fall after a distribution increase
body.explanation: REITs compete with bonds and FDs for income-seeking investors. When interest rates rise, investors demand a higher yield from REITs, so unit prices fall even when the underlying business is healthy.

body.text: In Chapter 2, a ₹1.2 crore strata office in Baner earned 8% until one tenant left and the year's yield collapsed to 1.87%. A REIT spreads the same risk across hundreds of tenants. One tenant leaving barely moves the distribution. That is the single biggest reason REITs usually suit individual investors better than a lone commercial unit.

body.title: The retired couple's ₹50 lakh
body.scenario: Suresh and Lata, both retired in Pune, have ₹50 lakh they want to turn into regular income. A relative suggests buying a small flat in Hinjewadi to rent out for about ₹18,000 a month. Their daughter suggests spreading the money across listed REITs instead.
body.prompt: How should they compare the two options?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Income: ₹18,000 a month is ₹2.16 lakh a year, a 4.3% gross yield. After maintenance, vacancy, repairs and property tax, it may fall to roughly 3%. REITs at roughly 5% to 7% could produce ₹2.5 to 3.5 lakh a year before tax, paid quarterly.
2. Costs: buying the flat costs about 7% or more in stamp duty and charges, around ₹3.5 lakh upfront. REIT units cost only brokerage and exchange charges.
3. Effort and risk: a flat means tenants, repairs and possible vacancy for a retired couple. REITs spread risk across many Grade A buildings and tenants.
4. Liquidity: if they need ₹10 lakh for a medical emergency, they can sell REIT units in a day. They cannot sell 20% of a flat.
5. What REITs add: price volatility they can see daily, sensitivity to interest rates, distributions that can change, and tax on each component.
6. Reasonable approach: REITs look better suited for regular income with less hassle, but they should not put all ₹50 lakh into REITs either. A mix with debt instruments like FDs or senior citizen schemes, after checking tax and consulting an adviser, would be more balanced.

body.title: Evaluating a REIT Before You Buy
steps: Check the distribution yield over the last four quarters and whether payouts are stable
Look at occupancy and WALE in the latest investor presentation
Compare the unit price with the latest NAV per unit
Review borrowing levels against the regulatory cap
Check tenant concentration and the share of rent from the top 10 tenants
Note which cities and asset types the REIT is exposed to
Read the distribution breakdown to estimate your after-tax yield
Spread money across more than one REIT if you want broader exposure

points: A REIT lets you own a share of Grade A office parks and malls through units traded on NSE and BSE.
SEBI rules keep REITs focused on completed, rent-earning assets and require at least 90% of distributable cash to be paid out.
India has six listed REITs as of mid-2026, which distributed ₹3,136 crore in Q1 FY27; five are office REITs and one owns malls.
From January 2026, mutual funds treat REITs as equity, and REITs became eligible for equity indices from July 2026.
Compared with a strata office unit, REITs offer small tickets, diversification, low transaction costs and daily liquidity.
REITs still carry interest rate, occupancy, sponsor and tax risks; judge them on yield, occupancy, WALE, NAV and debt.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. REITs named here are examples, not recommendations. Unit prices, yields and distributions change, and past distributions do not guarantee future payouts. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before investing.
